rows.title: Head movement
rows.text: Herons, storks and cranes bob their heads as they walk, and if you are a gray heron, little egret, intermediate egret, Pacific reef heron or Tick Bird, the most common pattern is one bob per step. If you are a Eurasian coot or a common moorhen, you bob your head while swimming as well as while walking. For most other waders, nobody has recorded how your head moves.
rows.note: Fixed "grey" to "gray" and the Pacific reef heron name. Left out field-of-view figures because numbers do not carry between species.

rows.title: Speed
rows.text: A lamp flashing 60 times a second looks steady to a human, but a bird's eyes may follow faster flashes. If you are a rock pigeon, you see a light flicker up to about 75 flashes a second, and if you are a domestic chicken, up to about 85. Nobody has measured how fast a flash you can follow if you are a heron, an egret, a crane or most other birds.
rows.note: Removed the phrase mentioning the view. Flicker speed carries only within a genus, so no heron or crane figure is stated. The chicken's 87 is rounded to 85.

rows.title: Sharpness
rows.text: If you are a rock pigeon, you read about 12 cycles a degree, and if you are a mourning dove, about 7, where a human reads about 30. Nobody has measured how sharply you see if you are any other kind of bird, a heron, egret or crane included.
rows.note: No record gives interreceptor angle for any species, so it is left out. Records for grouse, partridge and peafowl were not used because they are not relatives under the carry rules.

rows.title: Ultraviolet
rows.text: Nobody has measured how much ultraviolet, the light humans cannot see at all, reaches the eyes of a heron, egret, coot or dove, or how well they sense it. The shortest-wavelength color-sensing cell has been measured in the rock pigeon and the wild turkey, and in both it peaks in violet, at about 410 and 420 nanometers. In the whooping crane it peaks at about 405, so if you are a sandhill crane you very likely have a similar cell.
rows.note: Left out the peafowl and quail figures, since they belong to those species. No record gives an ultraviolet range for any heron, crane, pigeon or turkey.

rows.title: Field of view
rows.text: In the herons, egrets, moorhens and pigeons that have been measured, the part where both eyes see the same thing is a narrow upright strip in front of the bill, between about 20 and 35 degrees wide. If you are a black-crowned night heron, your two eyes together take in about 320 degrees around your head, and if you are a moorhen, about 300 degrees with a blind area behind your head. For most other waders, including the great blue heron, nobody has measured how wide your field of view is.

cites.taxon: Bubulcus ibis, Ardeola ralloides, Egretta gularis

rows.note: Left out the family-wide heron field width (R23, R24) and crane figure (R7) because field widths travel only within a genus.
